quickReset.name: Quick Reset
quickReset.description: Quick technique for a short pause

boxBreathing.title: Box Breathing (4-4-4-4)
boxBreathing.description: All four phases are equal. This steady rhythm helps you focus and stay calm; it is taught to military and emergency teams, among others.
boxBreathing.bestFor: Best for: Focus, concentration, stress management

calming.title: 4-7-8 Calming
calming.description: A short pause with full lungs, then a long out-breath. Many people find this rhythm especially soothing, particularly before sleep. If the pause feels uncomfortable, shorten it.
calming.bestFor: Best for: Anxiety relief, sleep preparation, deep relaxation

energizing.title: 4-4-6 Energizing
energizing.description: A balanced rhythm, neither too slow nor too fast, to regain some energy and clarity without getting out of breath.
energizing.bestFor: Best for: Mental clarity, energy boost, midday reset

quickReset.title: 3-3-3 Quick Reset
quickReset.description: A short rhythm for a quick pause when you only have a minute or two.
quickReset.bestFor: Best for: Quick stress relief, emergency calm, busy schedules

howItWorks.title: How Guided Breathing Works
howItWorks.description1: Following a set rhythm — such as 4-7-8 or box breathing — gives your breathing a slow, steady pace. Deliberately slowing your breathing often helps the body leave the alert state and relax.
howItWorks.description2: The rhythms offered serve different purposes: an even rhythm (box breathing) helps you focus, a longer out-breath (4-7-8) invites deeper relaxation, a short rhythm (3-3-3) takes only a minute or two. Choose the one that suits you best.
howItWorks.description3: Counting keeps the mind busy: while it follows the rhythm, it steps away a little from anxious thoughts.

rhythmicControl.title: A rhythm to follow
rhythmicControl.description: Following a set count gives the mind an anchor and helps the body slow down.

patternVariety.title: Several rhythms
patternVariety.description: Even rhythm to focus, long out-breath to relax, short rhythm when time is short.

neuralRegulation.title: A moment to relax
neuralRegulation.description: Slow, steady breathing supports relaxation and a calmer heart rate.

science.title: What Studies Say
science.description: Slow breathing is one of the most studied techniques. Syntheses of many studies show a moderate but real effect on stress and anxiety.
science.bottomLine: slow breathing is a simple, safe technique that helps many people feel calmer. It complements professional support but does not replace it.

meta.title: What many studies show
meta.who: About 800 adults for stress, in trials with healthy people or people with health conditions.
meta.what: Researchers pooled trials comparing breathing exercises (mostly slow breathing) with no exercise.
meta.result: Breathing reduced stress, anxiety and low mood. The effect is small to medium: useful, but not dramatic.
meta.caution: Study quality varied, and little is known about how long the effect lasts.

review.title: In people with an anxiety disorder
review.who: Adults with an anxiety disorder diagnosed by a doctor.
review.what: 16 studies testing breathing exercises on their own, without other treatment.
review.result: Overall, breathing exercises improved anxiety symptoms.
review.caution: The studies varied widely, and some results remain contradictory.

hospital.title: In hospitalised patients
hospital.who: 60 adults hospitalised with COVID-19 in a hospital in Iran.
hospital.what: Guided breathing exercises, 4 times a day for 5 days, compared with usual care.
hospital.result: Anxiety dropped clearly in patients who did the exercises (by about 40%), but not in the others.
hospital.caution: A single hospital and a very specific situation; the exercises also included respiratory physiotherapy.

whenToPractice.title: When to Practice
items: When you feel anxious or overwhelmed and need a pause
Before sleep, to quiet racing thoughts
In a stressful situation or before an important moment
Every day, so the technique becomes a reflex

whatYoullNotice.title: What You Might Notice
items: A sense of calm settling in after a few minutes
A slower heart rate and easing tension
Thoughts that quieten down a little
With regular practice, a technique that is easier to reach in difficult moments

technique.title: Technique
technique.description: Start with one pattern for at least a week before trying others. Consistency with a single technique builds deeper familiarity and effectiveness.

environment.title: Environment
environment.description: Find a quiet space where you won't be interrupted. Sit comfortably with your back supported and shoulders relaxed.

progression.title: Progression
progression.description: Begin with shorter sessions (2-3 minutes) and gradually extend as comfort increases. Don't force the breath—find your natural rhythm within the pattern.
